title: Lost in Tokyo
text: My first evening in Tokyo was supposed to be simple. I had arrived at six, left my suitcase at the hostel and gone out to find something to eat. I had a map, a phone with ten per cent of its battery left, and the confidence of someone who has read a great deal about a place and never actually been there. Within an hour I had walked into a department store, taken the wrong exit and discovered that Tokyo's streets have no names, at least none that a visitor can read.

I decided to take the train, which turned out to be an adventure in itself. The ticket machine offered a language I couldn't read, and the map on the wall looked like a bowl of coloured spaghetti. Around me, hundreds of people moved in complete silence, each of them looking as if they knew exactly where they were going. A schoolgirl in uniform, noticing my confusion, said something in careful English and led me to the platform. She even wrote the name of my station on a scrap of paper. I thanked her so many times that she laughed and hurried away, probably wondering what she had done to deserve it.

Unfortunately, I got off at the wrong station. The paper had said 'Ueno', but I had misread one letter and found myself in a district I had never heard of. It was nearly ten o'clock, my phone had died, and the streets were almost empty. I was hungry and tired, and for the first time since landing I felt a little frightened. Then I noticed a small, brightly lit shop, and the man behind the counter, who must have seen the look on my face, waved me inside. In his window stood rows of tiny plastic dishes, so realistic that I stared at them for a while.

He spoke no English and I spoke no Japanese, but we managed. He poured me a cup of green tea, then a bowl of noodles that he said, with gestures, was a gift. I tried to pay, and he shook his head firmly. Meanwhile, his wife telephoned someone, and ten minutes later a young man arrived. He was their nephew, a student who had spent a year in Canada. He listened to my story, laughed kindly and offered to take me back to the hostel.

We walked for twenty minutes, since the last train had gone, and talked the whole way. The night was warm, and the pavements smelled of rain and frying onions. He showed me a tiny shrine between two office buildings, a vending machine that sold hot coffee in cans, and a park where, even at that hour, a man was practising the violin. I realised that I had seen more of the real city in this accidental walk than I would have seen in a week of guided tours. At the hostel, he refused all thanks and simply wrote his email address on my hand.

I still have the scrap of paper from the schoolgirl and the email address of the nephew, with whom I exchange messages every month. People often ask me what I remember best about Japan, expecting me to mention temples or the speed of the trains. I tell them about the shop with the noodles. Getting lost, I now believe, is the best way to find out what a country is really like, as long as you don't mind asking for help. My friends say that I have turned the story into a legend, and perhaps they are right.

questions.q: What does the author mean by 'the confidence of someone who has read a great deal about a place and never actually been there'?
options: He was afraid of losing his way in a foreign city.
He had studied the history of the city at university.
He had prepared a detailed plan for the evening.
His reading made him feel sure he knew the city.

questions.q: What does the author say about the schoolgirl who helped him at the station?
options: She expected him to pay her something for her trouble.
She was surprised by how much he thanked her.
She was on her way home from school.
She spoke perfect English.

questions.q: Why did the author get off at the wrong station?
options: He had misread a note he was given.
The train had stopped earlier than planned.
The girl had made a mistake.
He had fallen asleep on the train.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT mentioned in paragraph 4?
options: A hot drink for him.
A meal offered as a present.
A journey by taxi.
A telephone call.

questions.q: The phrase 'this accidental walk' in paragraph 5 refers to ...
options: the first trip out of the hostel in search of dinner.
the return on foot with the shopkeeper's nephew.
the search for the right station.
a guided tour arranged by the hostel.

questions.q: What does the author remember best about Japan?
options: The ancient temples he visited during his stay.
How fast and punctual the trains were.
The beauty of the parks.
The kindness of the family in the shop.

questions.q: What conclusion does the author draw in the last paragraph?
options: Unplanned events show a visitor what a place is like.
Visitors should avoid public transport.
Guidebooks are more reliable than people.
It is dangerous to travel abroad without a charged phone.

discuss: Have you ever been lost in an unfamiliar place? What happened?
The author trusted strangers. When is it right to ask a stranger for help?
What would you most like to see in Japan?
